title: The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Financial Stability Board (FSB Secretariat; no individual authors named)
institution: Financial Stability Board (FSB)
type: international standard-setter report to the G20
verification: WebFetch read the FSB publication page and summary on 2026-11-05
relevance: The FSB's flagship assessment of how banks, insurers and asset managers are adopting AI and what that means for financial stability, updating its 2017 report for the generative-AI era. It identifies vulnerabilities with systemic potential: third-party dependencies and provider concentration, market correlations from herding on similar models, cyber risks, and model risk, data quality and governance weaknesses, plus GenAI-enabled fraud and disinformation. Benefits are framed as operational efficiency, compliance, product customisation and advanced analytics. It recommends that authorities close information gaps, monitor AI developments, review policy adequacy and build supervisory capacity, including with AI-powered tools.

title: Annual Economic Report 2024, Chapter III: Artificial intelligence and the economy — implications for central banks
authors: Bank for International Settlements (BIS Economic Department)
institution: Bank for International Settlements (BIS)
verification: WebFetch read the BIS chapter page on 2026-11-05
relevance: The most-cited macro-financial treatment of AI by a central-bank institution. It cites global AI spending topping US$150 billion in 2023, roughly 70% of financial-services firms using AI for cash-flow prediction, liquidity management, credit scoring and fraud detection, and a BIS-Ant Group field experiment (CodeFuse LLM) showing a 55% average programmer productivity gain concentrated among junior staff. It argues AI's short-run inflation impact depends on whether households anticipate the gains, and flags herding, algorithmic collusion, prompt injection and data poisoning as stability risks. It ends with an action plan for central banks centred on data governance and a 'community of practice'.

relevance: A pre-registered RCT that assigned 1,935 smallholder rice farmers in the Philippines and India over one production season to a personalized generative-AI advisory service or to a control chatbot without agronomic advice. relevance: A field survey of 305 cassava farmers across three Agricultural Development Poles in Benin, using a binary logit model to explain uptake of the PlantVillage Nuru smartphone AI app for cassava mosaic disease diagnosis. relevance: The judicial inquiry into Australia's automated 'income averaging' welfare debt-recovery scheme, which the report found produced inaccurate results and did not comply with the Social Security Act; debts raised wholly or partly by averaging were later reduced to zero and the scheme ended in 2019-2020. It remains the canonical case study of automated harms in benefits administration and the politics of algorithmic accountability.

relevance: The UK's independent audit of how central government is positioning itself to capture AI value in public services. It found AI not yet widely used, but 70% of surveyed bodies piloting or planning AI, and 37% of the 87 responding bodies already deploying AI across 74 use cases. title: AI Adoption in Developing Countries: Lessons from the Adoption of other Advanced Digital Technologies
authors: Xavier Cirera, Diego Comin, Marcio Cruz, Kyungmin Lee
institution: World Bank (Development Research Group / Digital Development); Dartmouth College
verification: Downloaded the 34-page World Bank working paper PDF and extracted title page and abstract with pypdf on 2026-11-05
relevance: A World Bank working paper (Cirera, Comin, Cruz and Lee) asking whether developing-country firms will adopt AI differently than they did earlier digital technologies. It mines the Firm Adoption of Technology (FAT) survey of more than 20,000 firms across income levels, plus new AI-adoption evidence from Romania. Findings: advanced digital technologies diffuse more slowly and are used less intensively in lower-income countries; intensive use predicts productivity better than adoption alone; AI adoption is concentrated among larger, better-managed, technologically advanced firms with little sign of leapfrogging; and AI is associated mainly with worker reassignment rather than net displacement. The punchline for policy is a 'dual gap' of adoption and use that complementary digital, managerial and workforce capabilities must close.

authors: OECD Secretariat (with support from ESRC UK, Austrian and German labour ministries, Employment and Social Development Canada)
institution: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
verification: Downloaded the 53-page OECD PDF and extracted the executive summary with pypdf on 2026-11-05
relevance: A late-2024 OECD survey of over 5,000 SMEs in Austria, Canada, Germany, Ireland, Japan, Korea and the UK - the closest thing to a comparative official census of generative-AI use in small firms. Generative AI is used in 31% of SMEs (24% in Japan to 39% in Germany); 65% of using SMEs say it increased employee performance, while 35% say it helped them scale up and 26% increased revenue. On jobs: 83% report no effect on overall staff need (6% increase, 9% decrease), 39% of skill-gap-affected SMEs say GenAI helped compensate for skill shortages, and twice as many SMEs associate GenAI with increased rather than decreased skill needs. Limitations: seven mostly high-income countries, self-reports, and survey period 2024 - so informal-economy firms are outside the frame.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of AI-assisted chest X-ray interpretation tools for TB screening: a rapid HTA
authors: Devang Raval, Dhaval Parmar, Somen Saha, Raju Sarkar, Medha Wadhwa, Apurvakumar Pandya, Harsh Shah, Kavitha Rajsekar
institution: Indian Institute of Public Health Gandhinagar (IIPHG); Department of Health Research, Government of India
verification: WebFetch read the full Frontiers in Digital Health article on 2026-11-05
relevance: An Indian rapid HTA comparing the AI chest X-ray readers qXR and Genki against radiologist interpretation for TB screening, using retrospective 2023 programme data from Maharashtra (6,281 patients) and Chennai (93,486 patients). Cost per interpreted case fell from INR 100 (US$1.21) for radiologists to INR 30 (US$0.36) for qXR and INR 22 (US$0.26) for Genki; qXR was cost-saving and Genki cost-effective against India's 2022 per-capita-GDP willingness-to-pay threshold (INR 197,440). Pooled accuracy: qXR sensitivity 90.22% and specificity 68.21%; Genki 90.41% and 66.38%; radiologist 88.72% and 49.61%. Authors flag provider-perspective-only costing and reliance on secondary cost data as limitations.

relevance: A retrospective costing of 66 community lung-health camps over 142 days in Nigeria's Gombe and Adamawa states, where 5,297 people were screened with an ultraportable X-ray plus the qXR AI reader and 85 bacteriologically confirmed TB cases were found. Cost per case detected ranged from US$1,198 (cough-only screening) to US$635 (any-symptom screening), with combined symptom-plus-CXR-AI around US$773 while detecting all 85 cases. title: Long-Term Outcomes and Cost-Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence for Breast Cancer Screening: A Modeling Study
authors: Matthew Andersen, Natalia Kunst, Ilana B. Richman
institution: Yale School of Medicine; University of York
verification: WebFetch read the Europe PMC REST record (PMID 40983310) with abstract on 2026-11-05; PubMed page itself blocked by a cookie notice
relevance: A microsimulation model (SEER, Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium and AI performance data) comparing biennial DBT screening alone versus DBT plus the Saige-Dx AI product in women aged 40-74. Per 1,000 women screened over a lifetime, AI cut false negatives by 2.1 and false positives by 49, added 3.09 QALYs, averted 0.13 breast-cancer deaths, but raised costs by US$936,430 - an ICER of US$303,279 per QALY. In 98% of simulations AI was not cost-effective at a US$100,000/QALY threshold, and results were insensitive to plausible test-characteristic changes, so the negative result is driven by pricing. As a US-priced modeling study it is the sharpest published counterweight to AI-detection trial optimism, complementing the RCT evidence already in the catalogue.

relevance: The first field study of legal-aid lawyers using generative AI, plus a survey of 202 legal-aid professionals, aimed at the roughly 90% of low-income Americans who lack adequate legal assistance. title: Resolução CNJ nº 615, de 11 de março de 2025 (diretrizes para desenvolvimento, utilização e governança de inteligência artificial no Poder Judiciário)
authors: Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ), signed by President Min. Luís Roberto Barroso
institution: Conselho Nacional de Justiça (National Council of Justice), Brazil
verification: WebFetch read the official CNJ act page (atos.cnj.jus.br, act 6001) on 2026-11-05
relevance: Brazil's binding nationwide rules for AI across every court in the world's largest judiciary, replacing the 2020 resolution and extending explicitly to generative AI and LLMs. It creates a risk annex (high-risk uses AR1-AR5 such as behavioural profiling, evidence weighting and conclusive legal judgments; low-risk uses like summarisation and drafting), mandates human oversight at all stages, and prohibits autonomous AI judicial decisions - 'vedada a utilização como instrumento autônomo de tomada de decisões judiciais' - with the judge fully responsible. It bans emotion recognition and criminality prediction, requires algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk systems, registration on the Sinapses platform, and adverse-incident reporting within 72 hours. A rare complete oversight architecture from a Global South judiciary, in force since July 2025 and amended by Resolution 674 of March 2026.

title: Is AI a key driving force for Chinese total factor productivity growth? Mechanistic analysis of employment, supply chain, and information asymmetry
authors: Ruifeng Xu, Frank M. Song
institution: Economic Modelling (Elsevier), Volume 150
verification: WebFetch read the IDEAS/RePEc abstract page (volume 150, 2025) on 2026-11-05; ScienceDirect full text redirected to an Elsevier sign-in; Crossref API confirmed metadata (title, authors, date September 2025)
relevance: An empirical study linking AI-patent data to financial records of Chinese listed firms, estimating AI-driven innovation's contribution to total factor productivity growth through employment, supply-chain optimisation and reduced information asymmetry. Its headline claim is that AI patents enhance productivity at roughly 40 times the rate of ordinary patents, with the effect strongest where firms hire more highly educated workers, and with implications for aging-population and middle-income-trap risks. Heterogeneity analyses find computer-system AI patents most valuable. Limitations: listed-firm sample skews large, patent-based AI measurement is an imperfect proxy for adoption, and the 40x ratio is a model-dependent comparison rather than a causal field estimate.

authors: Hilmy Prilliadi

relevance: An ERIA policy brief projecting AI adoption to contribute 10-18% of ASEAN's GDP (AI market of about US$30.3 billion by 2030), with manufacturing, healthcare and energy named as the biggest beneficiary sectors.
